title: Walking in Love and Light; Christ and the Church
summary: Paul calls believers to imitate God and walk in love as Christ loved us, to leave behind sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, and to live as children of light who expose the deeds of darkness. They are to walk wisely, be filled with the Spirit, sing to one another, give thanks, and submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. That call then opens the instructions on marriage: wives are to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, a union Paul calls a profound mystery that speaks of Christ and the church.
story: Chapter 4 began the letter's practical half with unity and the call to put on the new self. Chapter 5 continues the pattern with three more pictures of the Christian walk: walk in love (v. 2), walk as children of light (v. 8), and walk wisely (v. 15). The Spirit-filled life described in verses 18 to 21 then opens into the household instructions that run to 6:9, addressing wives and husbands here, and children, parents, slaves, and masters in chapter 6. Marriage is not treated as a separate topic but as one of the places where the gospel is lived out, and Paul reaches back to Genesis 2:24 to show that God's design for marriage from the beginning pointed to Christ and his people.
historical:
Discussions of household management were common in the ancient world. Aristotle, writing in the fourth century BC, treated the household in terms of three pairs of relationships: master and slave, husband and wife, father and children, with the male head of household ruling in each. Later Greek, Roman, and Jewish writers continued the tradition. The Roman household (familia) was headed by the father (paterfamilias), who held extensive legal power over his wife, children, and slaves. Scholars call Paul's instructions here, and parallel passages in Colossians 3:18-4:1 and 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, household codes, because they follow this familiar pattern.

What stands out is how Paul changes it. He addresses wives, children, and slaves directly, as responsible members of the church, which ordinary household codes rarely did. He puts duties on the husband, father, and master as well, and the husband's duty is not to rule but to love to the point of self-sacrifice. And he frames the whole passage with the command to submit to one another (v. 21), which many read as mutual submission among all believers and others as each yielding to those set over them in the relationships that follow.
cultural:
Marriage in the Greek and Roman world was often arranged by families for reasons of property and alliance. Wives were expected to obey, and husbands commonly held a double standard in sexual matters; Roman law and custom tolerated a husband's use of slaves and prostitutes. Against that background Paul's command that husbands love their wives as their own bodies, and as Christ loved the church, set a demanding standard for men.

The warning against drunkenness (v. 18) would have been pointed in a city where feasts, drinking parties, and the worship of Dionysus, the god of wine, were part of public life. Paul contrasts being filled with wine with being filled with the Spirit, which shows itself in singing, thanksgiving, and mutual submission rather than in excess. The washing with water (v. 26) may echo the bridal bath taken before a wedding in both Jewish and Greek custom, and many readers also hear a reference to baptism.
literary: The first part of the chapter (vv. 1-20) continues the walk language of chapter 4, with sharp contrasts between light and darkness, wise and foolish, drunkenness and the Spirit. Verse 14 quotes a saying, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you”, whose source is not known; many scholars think it comes from an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism. Verses 18 to 21 form one long sentence in Greek: the command be filled with the Spirit is followed by a series of participles (speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting) that describe what the Spirit's filling looks like. In some of the earliest Greek manuscripts verse 22 has no verb of its own; wives, to your husbands borrows submit from verse 21. This ties the household instructions grammatically to verse 21. The passage on marriage (vv. 22-33) moves back and forth between husband and wife and Christ and the church, then quotes Genesis 2:24 and names the mystery.

outline.t: Imitate God and walk in love
Walk wisely, filled with the Spirit, submitting to one another
Wives and husbands: the church and Christ
Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church

doctrines.note: Marriage is presented as a living picture of Christ's union with the church. The husband's love is measured by Christ's self-giving, and the wife's response by the church's relation to Christ. Christians differ on how the roles in this passage apply today (see the hard question), but the passage plainly lifts marriage into the center of Christian discipleship.
Be filled with the Spirit (v. 18) is a continuing command. The Spirit's filling shows itself not in spectacle but in worship, gratitude, and submission to one another.
Believers are to have no part in sexual immorality, impurity, or greed, which Paul equates with idolatry (v. 5). Holiness is presented as living as what they already are, children of light.
Christ loved the church, gave himself for her, cleanses her, and will present her to himself radiant and holy (vv. 25-27). The church is Christ's bride and body, nourished and cherished by him.

words.note: Hupotasso, to submit, to place oneself under, or to arrange in order. It appears in verse 21 for all believers toward one another and in verse 24 for wives toward husbands and the church toward Christ. In Paul the middle form describes voluntary yielding, not forced subjection. How mutual submission (v. 21) relates to the specific call to wives (vv. 22-24) is at the center of the passage's debate.

Kephale, head. Literally the physical head; figuratively it can mean a leader or ruler, and some scholars argue it can also carry the sense of source or origin, as the head of a river. Complementarian interpreters generally hold that authority is the main sense here; egalitarian interpreters often emphasize source, or a head that nourishes and serves the body, as Christ does (vv. 23, 29). The word's range in Greek literature is itself debated.

Agapao, to love. It appears seven times in the chapter. Believers are to walk in love as Christ loved us (v. 2), and husbands are to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (v. 25). The measure of love here is not feeling but self-giving sacrifice.

Musterion, mystery, a purpose of God once hidden and now revealed. In verse 32 the mystery is that the union of husband and wife in Genesis 2:24 speaks of Christ and the church. Marriage from the beginning was designed to point beyond itself.

christ: The chapter holds up Christ's love as the pattern for all Christian conduct. He loved us and gave himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God (v. 2), language drawn from Israel's sacrifices. In the marriage passage Christ is the head and Savior of the church, who loved her, gave himself for her, cleanses her by the word, and will present her to himself glorious and blameless (vv. 23-27). He nourishes and cherishes her as his own body (v. 29). Paul's quotation of Genesis 2:24 finds in the first marriage a picture of this union. The Old Testament prophets had already described God as Israel's husband (Hosea 2; Isaiah 54:5), and the New Testament presents Jesus as the bridegroom who fulfills that picture (Mark 2:19; Revelation 19:7).

hard.q: What does it mean for wives to submit and husbands to be the head, and how should the passage be read today?
hard.a:
This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, and faithful Christians read it in two main ways.

Complementarians hold that God created men and women equal in dignity and worth but with different roles, and that this passage teaches a lasting pattern in marriage: the husband is to lead his wife in self-sacrificial love modeled on Christ, and the wife is to respond by willingly submitting to that leadership as the church does to Christ. They note that Paul grounds the pattern not in Roman culture but in Christ and the church and in Genesis 2, which suggests it is meant to outlast its first setting. They insist, as the text does, that headship is never license for harshness, domination, or abuse, and that the husband's calling to die to himself is the heavier one.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and in role, and that verse 21, submit to one another, governs the whole passage. They read Paul's instructions to wives as working within the patriarchal household of his day while transforming it from the inside, much as he regulated slavery in 6:5-9 without endorsing it. On this reading the direction of the gospel, seen in the command to husbands to love sacrificially and in texts such as Galatians 3:28, points toward marriages of mutual submission, and applying the passage today means following that direction rather than preserving the ancient structure. Many egalitarians also argue that head may mean source or one who nourishes.

Both readings agree on much: marriage mirrors Christ's love for the church; the husband's love must be costly and self-giving; the passage gives no cover for control or abuse; and wives and husbands alike stand before Christ as full members of his body. Where they differ is a second-order question on which believers who equally honor Scripture have reached different conclusions.

questions: Paul contrasts being drunk with wine and being filled with the Spirit. What does it look like, in ordinary life, to be filled with the Spirit?
Verse 21 calls all believers to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Where is that call most difficult for you?
Paul measures a husband's love by Christ's love for the church. What would change in any close relationship if that were the measure of love?
